title: The Didache: two ways
hookLine: an early handbook: there are two ways, of life and of death; pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day

cards: A short book, only a handful of pages, and it isn't in the Bible. It's more like a church's handbook: what to teach new believers, how to baptize, when to fast, how to pray, what to do with traveling preachers.
Its title calls it the teaching of the twelve apostles. It's very practical. If a traveling apostle stays more than a couple of days, or asks for money, the book says, he's a false prophet.
Somebody had clearly met that guy. But the book doesn't open with rules. It opens with a choice.

teach.b: The word is Didache, Greek for teaching, and its first line says there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and a great difference between them. The picture isn't new.
Moses says in Deuteronomy: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life."
Jeremiah too: "Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death." Jews and Christians share the image.
Then the Didache describes the way of life, and it sounds like the Sermon on the Mount turned into a checklist for beginners. Love God who made you. Love your neighbor as yourself.
Whatever you wouldn't want done to you, don't do to another. Bless those who curse you. Pray for your enemies.
Give to everyone who asks. The way of death is the list of what breaks people: lies, greed, cruelty, pride. Later the handbook turns to prayer.

teach.h: THE LORD'S PRAYER, THREE TIMES A DAY.
teach.b: It gives the Lord's Prayer from Matthew's Gospel, "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name," with a short line of praise at the end, and a plain instruction: pray it three times a day. Not a new prayer.
The same one, three times over, so the day has a shape.
The Didache isn't part of the Bible, but it's a window into how some early Christians tried to live: two ways, and a prayer said again and again to stay on one of them.

how: Some Christians pray the Lord's Prayer at set times through the day, and churches that pray morning and evening prayer include it in each service; the Didache is read today as an early Christian writing, not as scripture.

practice: If you pray, say the Lord's Prayer once now, slowly, one line per breath, letting each line land before the next. If you don't, read or recall its lines slowly as words, and notice which one catches.
Either way, let the last line rest a moment before you move on.
